newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurdish fighters set for north Iraq showdown.
newsitem.headline: Kurdish fighters set for north Iraq showdown.

text.p: Rival Kurdish militias were set for a showdown on Wednesday in fighting in northern Iraq that has worried Washington, the Kurds' nominal protector against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
Several thousand Kurdish guerrillas known as "peshmergas" (those who face death) from two feuding factions were ranged against each other near the town of Degala.

The pro-Baghdad Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) of Massoud Barzani forced its Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) opponents back 10 km (six miles) in a counter-attack on Tuesday and promised a further push.
"We are now just waiting for a new order to continue our final attack to Koy Sanjak," said Robitran Ibrahim, commander of KDP forces in Degala.
Koy Sanjak is the home town of veteran PUK leader Jalal Talabani and lies on a strategically important road.
PUK forces said they had pulled back only to regroup for an imminent drive on the city of Arbil, captured by the KDP in late August with the help of Iraqi troops and weapons.

"Now our target is Arbil," senior PUK leader Kosrat Rasoul told Reuters, contradicting comments from Talabani who has said he will not move on the city, the seat of a regional Kurdish parliament that fell apart last year.
"We are here to start our final attack towards Arbil," a PUK guerrilla told Reuters in Koy Sanjak. He was one of around 3,000 fighters loyal to Talabani gathered in the town.
A KDP delegation was due in Washington on Wednesday for talks with State Department officials. The United States has called on both sides to return to the negotiating table.
Barzani's group, which says it is no longer dealing with Saddam, is to complain to the United States about what it says is Iranian military support for its rival.
Tehran and Talabani deny any military cooperation.
Washington launched waves of missiles against Iraqi military installations in retaliation for the fall of Arbil, which cost the United States much of its influence in the north.
U.S., British and French planes have been patrolling the skies of northern Iraq since the end of the Gulf War in 1991 to shield Iraq's Kurds from Baghdad.
The air force has played no part in the inter-Kurdish feud.
There was no sign of Iranian forces on Monday in Iraqi Kurdistan's biggest city Sulaimaniya, which the PUK took almost overnight last weekend.
Some 2,500 people shouting slogans against Barzani and Saddam demonstrated in the city near the Iranian border, witnesses said.
